column2: Welcome to the world of the Braille alphabet, where every letter and number is represented using 6 dots arranged in 2 columns and 3 rows, and counting goes by column (from top to bottom, the first column is 1, 2, and 3, and the second column, in the same order, is 4, 5, and 6 - as shown in the picture). The keyboard letters can also help you: F, D, S = dots 1, 2, and 3 (left hand), J, K, L = dots 4, 5, and 6 (right hand). In other words, for easier orientation, your left hand is for the first column and your right hand for the second; your index finger is for the first, topmost dot in the column (dots 1 and 4), your middle finger is for the second, middle dot in the columns (dots 2 and 5), and your ring finger is for the third, lowest dots in the columns (3 and 6).

Welcome to the world of the Braille alphabet, where every letter and number is represented using 6 dots arranged in 2 columns and 3 rows, and counting goes by column (from top to bottom, the first column is 1, 2, and 3, and the second column, in the same order, is 4, 5, and 6 - as shown in the picture). On the phone the dots are arranged just like on a braille writer: dots 1, 2 and 3 run along the left edge of the screen (left hand), and dots 4, 5 and 6 along the right edge (right hand). At the top are dots 1 and 4 - for your index fingers, in the middle are dots 2 and 5 - for your middle fingers, and at the bottom are dots 3 and 6 - for your ring fingers. The phone is easiest to use held with both hands or placed on a table in front of you. When you tap a dot, it lights up and the phone vibrates.
